overview: This 60-page file documents how U.S. diplomats and military and naval attachés monitored suspected Japanese activity in Costa Rica between 1932 and 1939, chiefly through the lens of Panama Canal security. Although early inquiries found no evidence of Japanese coastal surveying, later reports increasingly interpreted fishing enterprises, cotton cultivation schemes, commercial advertising, charitable donations, immigration proposals, and travel around Puntarenas, Guanacaste, and Golfo Dulce as possible instruments of propaganda, reconnaissance, colonization, or espionage. The file also follows Japanese interest in the financially troubled Pacific Refrigeration Company, Costa Rican responses to requests and investments, and Colonel Gerard F. Montúfar’s unsolicited warning about Japanese influence, while cross-references connect these developments to wider concerns about Japanese activities in Panama and Central America.
interest: Shows how routine commerce and migration became securitized in U.S. reports on Costa Rica before the war.
